clue.text: Capulet cat

definitions.meaning: Juliet's fiery cousin in Romeo and Juliet belongs to the Capulet household
Mercutio mocks him as 'Prince of Cats', and the name is the cat's in the Reynard fables

explanation.definitionFit: The same Shakespearean character is both a member of Juliet's family and the namesake of the fable cat Tibert.

clue.text: Kingsley work uses parts of Yeats

indicators.note: the poet's name is broken into parts and its letters reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist borrows pieces of an Irish poet for his book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts of' signals rearranging the letters of the poet's name. Charles Kingsley wrote the novel of that title in 1848.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley's first novel bears the title of the fermenting agent.

clue.text: Provenance of The Grail?

parts.note: legend says the holy cup was brought to Britain by Joseph, so its origin is his home town in Judea

explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, the man from this Judean town, is the legendary keeper of the holy cup, so the town is its supposed source.

clue.text: Language from quite lugubrious indian

indicators.note: the language is drawn out of the run of letters across these two words

explanation.surface: An Indian speaker comes across as rather gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells you to take the letters running across 'quite lugubrious'; 'indian' only confirms the language is from India.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dravidian tongue of Andhra Pradesh in southern India.

clue.text: Napoleon III took it on the chin

definitions.text: Napoleon III took it on the chin

parts.words: Napoleon III took it on the chin
parts.note: the emperor wore a small pointed tuft of beard below his lip, a style named after him and his title

explanation.definitionFit: The little chin beard is named for the emperor who made it fashionable.

clue.text: Edna Lyall's source book for Buñuel's L'Age d'Or?

definitions.text: Edna Lyall's source book for Buñuel's L'Age d'Or?

parts.words: Edna Lyall's source book for Buñuel's L'Age d'Or?
parts.note: the French film title means 'the golden age', so the joke pretends it was adapted from a Victorian novelist's book with a similar title

explanation.definitionFit: Edna Lyall wrote a novel of that title, and Buñuel's film title translates as an age of gold.

clue.text: Elements of diaspora in Italian poem

indicators.note: the letters, the elements of the word diaspora, are taken apart and arranged anew

explanation.surface: Scattered exile communities feature in a poem from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elements of' signals that the letters of 'diaspora' are rearranged. The definition is the third part of Dante's Divine Comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's Divine Comedy ends with this canticle about heaven.

clue.text: Rather mechanical player in Capek's R.U.R.

definitions.text: Rather mechanical player in Capek's R.U.R.

parts.words: Rather mechanical player in Capek's R.U.R.
parts.note: Karel Capek's play about artificial workers gave English the word for a machine-like man, so the stiff 'player' is literally one of them

explanation.definitionFit: Capek's 1920 play introduced the word for its manufactured workers.

clue.text: Friend of Sir Toby who combines fever with effrontery

parts.note: an ague is a malarial fever with shivering
cheek is impudent boldness

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean companion is described as feverish and impudent.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night Sir Toby Belch's foolish drinking companion is Sir Andrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Andrew is the gullible crony of Sir Toby Belch in Twelfth Night.

clue.text: One associated with magician subsequently becomes venerator of Virgin

parts.note: Thomas Mann's story is 'Mario and the Magician'
subsequently means later

explanation.surface: A conjuror's assistant later turns into a devotee of the Madonna.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'magician' is Cipolla in Thomas Mann's novella 'Mario and the Magician'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who worships Mary, mother of Jesus, excessively is so called.

clue.text: Tom Sharpe writes of steak this rare in France

definitions.text: Tom Sharpe writes of steak this rare in France

parts.words: Tom Sharpe writes of steak this rare in France
parts.note: Sharpe's Cambridge comedy is named for a porterhouse steak plus a colour, and French cooks call a very rare steak by that colour

explanation.definitionFit: Tom Sharpe's novel is Porterhouse Blue, and bleu is the French term for steak cooked very rare.

clue.text: "Ugly mists / Of vapors that did seem to — him" (King Henry IV, Part 1)

definitions.text: "Ugly mists / Of vapors that did seem to — him" (King Henry IV, Part 1)

parts.words: "Ugly mists / Of vapors that did seem to — him" (King Henry IV, Part 1)
parts.note: Prince Hal's soliloquy compares himself to the sun that breaks through clouds that seemed to choke it; the gap is the verb for choking

explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to throttle or choke, completing Hal's image of the smothered sun.

clue.text: Perceive what Sergeant Cuff did to find the

definitions.meaning: to perceive is to notice or discover

definitions.text: what Sergeant Cuff did to find the
definitions.meaning: Sergeant Cuff is the policeman investigating the stolen jewel in Wilkie Collins's novel, so he works as a sleuth

explanation.walkthrough: The clue appears to end in a cross-reference to the Collins novel at 14 that the text as held lost.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice is to discover something, which is a sleuth's job, as Cuff's is in Collins's novel.

clue.text: Nurse in Adam Aherne's new play

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the two words of the playwright's name

explanation.surface: A nurse appears in a new play by a dramatist called Adam Aherne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters running across 'Adam Aherne's'; 'new play' only dresses the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: In India and the Far East this word means a children's nurse or maid.

clue.text: Jewel of Collins's oeuvre

definitions.meaning: Wilkie Collins wrote the 1868 detective novel of that title

explanation.definitionFit: The title of Wilkie Collins's novel is also a pale opalescent gem.

clue.text: Haunted, like Lloyd C. Douglas's eye surgeon

definitions.text: like Lloyd C. Douglas's eye surgeon
definitions.meaning: the surgeon in Douglas's novel 'Magnificent Obsession' is driven by a single idea

explanation.definitionFit: Being preoccupied by one idea fits both a haunted mind and Douglas's driven doctor in Magnificent Obsession.

clue.text: They formed "a ghastly crew" in Coleridge

definitions.text: They formed "a ghastly crew" in Coleridge

parts.words: They formed "a ghastly crew" in Coleridge
parts.note: in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner the dead mariners rise to work the ship, and the poem calls them a ghastly crew

explanation.definitionFit: The ship's seamen, raised from the dead in Coleridge's poem, make up the ghastly crew.

clue.text: "… the very painting of your fear: / This is the — dagger" (Macbeth)

definitions.text: "… the very painting of your fear: / This is the — dagger" (Macbeth)

parts.words: "… the very painting of your fear: / This is the — dagger" (Macbeth)
parts.note: Lady Macbeth mocks her husband's vision of a knife traced in empty space; the gap is that hyphenated adjective

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a dagger sketched in thin air, imaginary rather than real.

clue.text: 28 is somehow a Shakespearean tomboy

indicators.note: somehow says those letters are put together in some new way

parts.note: the answer at 28 across is the name from the Leacock quotation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man's name is somehow turned into a boyish Shakespeare heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges RONALD (28 across) with IS. The heroine of As You Like It disguises herself as the youth Ganymede.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of As You Like It spends most of the play disguised as a young man.

clue.text: Colour of Hamlet's cloak

parts.note: in Act I Hamlet tells his mother that his mourning garment is black as writing fluid

explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet speaks of his 'inky cloak', black like writing fluid.

clue.text: Point to one in distress? (A crystal gazer)

parts.note: S is south, a compass point
someone in distress weeps, so is a crier, here spelt with Y

explanation.surface: A question about pointing to someone in trouble, with a fortune-teller added in brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass point gives S; the weeper is spelt CRYER, an accepted variant.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer foretells the future by gazing into a crystal ball.

clue.text: Pansy whose stepmother was one of the Archers

definitions.text: Pansy whose stepmother was one of the Archers

parts.words: Pansy whose stepmother was one of the Archers
parts.note: in Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady, Isabel Archer marries Gilbert, whose daughter is Pansy

explanation.walkthrough: 'the Archers' looks like the long-running BBC radio soap about a farming family; it is Isabel Archer's family in Henry James.
explanation.definitionFit: Pansy is Gilbert's daughter in The Portrait of a Lady, and Isabel Archer becomes her stepmother.

clue.text: Dramatist coming indirectly from Troon

indicators.note: taking a roundabout route, the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A playwright arrives by a roundabout way from a Scottish golfing town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'indirectly' rearranges the letters of TROON, a seaside golf town in Ayrshire, Scotland. Joe Orton wrote Loot.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Orton was the English playwright of Loot and Entertaining Mr Sloane.

clue.text: "--, how splendid to meet again after all these years", said Farebrother (Anthony Powell)

definitions.text: "--, how splendid to meet again after all these years", said Farebrother (Anthony Powell)

parts.words: "--, how splendid to meet again after all these years", said Farebrother (Anthony Powell)
parts.note: in A Dance to the Music of Time, Farebrother greets the narrator, surname Jenkins, by his first name

explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of Powell's sequence is Nick Jenkins, whom Farebrother greets by his full first name.

clue.text: A Welsh one mentions Arthur's death

definitions.text: A Welsh one mentions Arthur's death

parts.words: A Welsh one mentions Arthur's death
parts.note: the medieval ... Cambriae record the battle of Camlann where Arthur fell, so one year's entry in that chronicle is meant

explanation.definitionFit: A single year's record in a chronicle such as the Annales Cambriae, which notes Arthur's fall at Camlann.

clue.text: Eliot's hero in Tarka's home?

definitions.meaning: George Eliot's novel is Felix ..., the Radical
Tarka is Henry Williamson's otter, and an otter's den has that name

explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's radical Felix shares his surname with the word for an otter's lair.

clue.text: One name day derived from a surname of Venus

indicators.note: the epithet is made out of the letters of the preceding words, rearranged

explanation.surface: A feast day named after someone gives rise to a title of the goddess of love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'derived from' rearranges ONE, NAME and DAY. The Greek epithet means 'rising from the sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus Anadyomene, rising from the sea, is a classical title of the love goddess.

clue.text: Sussex schoolboy with a friend in Derbyshire, we hear

definitions.text: Sussex schoolboy with a friend in Derbyshire, we hear

parts.words: Sussex schoolboy with a friend in Derbyshire, we hear
parts.note: Anthony Buckeridge's boarding-school hero at Linbury Court in Sussex has a best friend named Darbishire, which sounds like the county

explanation.definitionFit: Buckeridge's schoolboy hero attends Linbury Court in Sussex with his friend Darbishire.

clue.text: "Lord… flung himself upon his horse and rode madly off in all directions" (Stephen Leacock)

definitions.text: "Lord… flung himself upon his horse and rode madly off in all directions" (Stephen Leacock)

parts.words: "Lord… flung himself upon his horse and rode madly off in all directions" (Stephen Leacock)
parts.note: the famous line comes from Leacock's 'Gertrude the Governess', about an impetuous young nobleman

explanation.definitionFit: The missing first name belongs to the hot-headed nobleman of Leacock's parody 'Gertrude the Governess'.
